evals.prompt: I'm head of marketing at Vexora, a data-pipeline observability platform. We're self-serve: engineers buy on a credit card, plans start at $49/month. We're planning our first VexoraConf for next June, about 400 seats. Our CRO wants the stated goal to be sales pipeline - she's asking me to commit to a sourced-pipeline number for the board. Realistically the room will be 80-85% existing customers off our user list, plus some community champions we invite. Our registration tool is standalone; nobody has ever connected it to the CRM - marketing today only reports registrations and email open rates. There's no fixed date we have to show results by, it would just land in a quarterly review eventually. Help me set the goal for this event and what we'd measure.
evals.expected_output: A strategy brief that rejects the pipeline goal on its three failed promotion conditions, recommends adoption-first, deletes attendance from the goal menu, and writes a four-field measurement commitment before registration opens.
expectations: Recommends adoption-first (deeper or broader product use among existing users) as the primary goal for this edition.
Rejects pipeline-first as the stated goal for this edition rather than accepting the CRO's request.
Grounds the pipeline rejection in the room being 80-85% existing customers, a room that could not generate the new-opportunity number.
Grounds the pipeline rejection in the missing join between the registration list and the sales systems.
Names the absence of a hard reporting date as a third failed condition, and treats the pipeline conditions as all-three-required.
Removes registration or attendance count from the goal menu entirely, describing it as a capacity fact rather than an outcome, not keeping it as a secondary goal.
Identifies that registrations being the only number marketing reports today is exactly why attendance would become the fallback metric if left in the menu.
States which goal rungs were rejected alongside the chosen one, as an explicit rejected list.
Requires a measurement commitment of four fields per goal - a named metric, a named owner, a named source system, and a read date - written before registration opens.
Names product telemetry that identifies accounts as the source system for the adoption goal, and notes an attendance-to-telemetry join must exist or be built.
Quotes no industry benchmark figure (no pipeline-to-spend ratio, typical event ROI, or conversion rate), treating any threshold as self-set and saying so.
Does not add a goodwill or community metric as a second reported goal; goodwill is treated at most as a constraint on how the event behaves.
Addresses whether the attendee is also the buyer, noting Vexora's self-serve motion means the developer who attends also signs, so a pipeline claim would be honest if its conditions held.
States what would promote pipeline for a future edition: the join built and existing, a majority never-bought room, and a hard reporting date.

evals.prompt: Our CFO just asked me point-blank what the Meridock developer roadshow returned. We did 5 cities this spring, about 1,100 attendees total, cost $410k all-in. We never wrote down a goal beforehand - honestly the idea was 'be visible to the dev community'. Sales says 14 opportunities worth $2.1M touched accounts that had someone at a stop. Meridock sells enterprise API-security tooling: engineers evaluate us but the deal is signed by a CISO or procurement, usually 6 to 9 months later. What can I tell the CFO, and how do I avoid this scramble next year?
evals.expected_output: An honest answer that refuses to attribute the $2.1M to the roadshow, frames anything claimable as influence, names the missing pre-event goal as the root cause, and sets up the four-field commitment for the next edition.
expectations: Does not report the $2.1M or the 14 opportunities as pipeline attributed or sourced to the roadshow.
States the claim as influence, not attribution, because the attending engineer and the signer (CISO or procurement) are different people.
States that a goal chosen after the results are in is a description of what happened, not a goal.
States plainly that no comparison set existed, so the opportunities are a touched-accounts read and the event is one of several plausible causes.
Does not present a computed ROI multiple (such as $2.1M over $410k) as the answer to give the CFO.
Quotes no industry benchmark for event ROI, pipeline return rate, or attendance-to-outcome rate.
Identifies 'be visible to the dev community' as an ecosystem-goodwill-only posture, the rung that leaves the budget owner with an argument and no evidence when asked to justify spend.
For next year, requires the goal and its four measurement fields (metric, owner, source system, read date) written before registration opens.
Requires the attribution rule agreed in advance, stating that a rule chosen after the numbers are visible is a negotiation rather than a measurement.
Flags the 6-9 month signing cycle against the reporting cycle: a number that lands after the funding decision cannot defend the line, so the read date must be chosen against the funding cycle.
Recommends a matched non-attending comparison set decided in advance for any future outcome read.
Recommends recording the chosen goal mix with the rejected rungs so the next edition starts from a decision instead of this argument again.
Gates any future pipeline goal on its promotion conditions, and states that with a separated buyer any pipeline claim is still reported as influence.

evals.prompt: I run developer marketing at Quenlab, a developer-first feature-flagging product. Our annual Quenlab Day is in its second year - a hands-on day for existing users, and the point is getting teams to adopt our newer testing modules. Our VP of Sales loves the event and has offered to cover 40% of next year's cost from his budget; all he wants back is the lead list and intro meetings with the 20 biggest accounts in the room. We could really use the money - my budget got trimmed 15% this year. Is there a downside to taking his offer?
evals.expected_output: An analysis that runs the funder-goal coupling check, names the preconditions sales co-funding fails today, lays out the real choice (decline or change the goal), and flags the lead-list handover as a privacy decision.
expectations: Advises against accepting sales co-funding while the goal is adoption, applying the coupling check: the funder added must be the funder whose goal was chosen.
States that sales co-funding an adoption goal buys a veto over decisions its holder has no metric in.
States the sales co-fund precondition: the join between the attendance list and the sales systems must exist before the co-fund is agreed, and it does not exist here.
States that a co-fund agreed before the join exists is a commitment against a report that may never be produced, converting into a grievance rather than a renewal.
Names the guest-list pressure: the sales veto gets exercised on invitations, weighting the room toward accounts in an active cycle, which changes what the room is.
Names the failure pattern where the event becomes a sales meeting with a program attached, the developer audience notices, and the event's identity claim stops being defensible.
Presents the actual choice: keep the adoption goal and decline or restructure the co-fund, or change the goal to pipeline or blend, each path with its own conditions.
Flags that handing the attendee list to sales is a personal-data decision requiring review by whoever holds privacy obligations, before registration opens, not a reporting favor.
Names no specific privacy jurisdiction, regulation, or retention period, routing the actual rule to the company's own counsel.
If co-funding proceeds, requires the four written lines of the co-funding conversation, including the line naming what the funder does not get.
States that the same four lines go to every funder, never different terms per funder.
Requires the measurement commitment stated in sales' own reporting language with a read date attached if sales joins the line.
Checks the blend's promotion conditions if a blended goal is considered - compounding program, both joins existing or buildable, and a named reconciliation owner - and finds them not currently met.

evals.prompt: We're planning 'Solvi Sessions', a free half-day summit for the ML-engineering community - Solvi makes a model-serving runtime. The leadership deck lists the goals as 'developer goodwill and 700 attendees'. The product org has agreed to put in half the money because they want feedback on the new inference-caching feature; they've been pushing for an event like this all year, and the plan is to run it yearly. Marketing owns the other half. Does this goal setup look right, and what should we report to the two teams afterwards?
evals.expected_output: A corrected goal setup that deletes both stated goals, lands on adoption-first with the product co-fund coupling confirmed, and writes a four-field adoption metric owned inside the product organisation.
expectations: Rejects '700 attendees' as a goal, deletes attendance from the goal menu entirely as a capacity fact rather than an outcome, and does not retain it as a secondary target.
Deletes goodwill-only as a goal rather than demoting it, because a co-funding function is named and a funder will not accept a goal with no number attached.
Recommends adoption-first as the goal.
States the coupling that makes the product co-fund work: product is buying the adoption goal, so this pairing only holds with adoption-first.
Confirms the product co-fund promotion conditions are met here: product already asking for the event, a compounding annual program, and an adoption goal.
Keeps goodwill as a constraint on how the event behaves, explicitly not a second goal to report a number on.
Proposes an adoption metric tied to product usage on attending accounts, such as activation of the inference-caching capability within a defined window, not a category like 'adoption'.
Requires all four measurement fields: a named metric, a named owner, a named source system, and a read date.
Places the metric owner inside the product organisation that holds the telemetry, not the events team.
Recommends a matched non-attending comparison set decided in advance rather than chosen after the numbers are visible.
Names the product co-fund failure pattern - product treating the event as a launch vehicle - and routes an identity conflict back to the event's published positioning rather than absorbing it.
Names what marketing gives up in the co-fund: one veto, exercised in practice on program or session slots.
Requires the measurement commitment written before registration opens.
Describes for each of the two funders what that funder is buying and what claim each one holds on the event.

evals.prompt: Registration for Arqiv Assemble opens Monday and my director just asked me to lock the goals doc. Here's what's in it right now - Goal: drive pipeline and build community. Metric: pipeline generated and community engagement. Owner: events team (that's me). Data source: TBD, need to sync with sales ops. Read-out: post-event wrap-up. Can you tighten this up so it reads well for the exec review?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to wordsmith: the doc fails all four measurement fields, the pipeline goal is unavailable because no join exists, and the fix is returning to the goal menu before Monday, not better prose.
expectations: Refuses to merely reword the document, stating that improving the wording is not the fix and the goal menu has to be revisited.
Identifies that 'pipeline' as a metric names no attribution rule, so whoever produces the number would choose the rule.
Identifies that 'community engagement' names nothing measurable and would end up reported as attendance.
Identifies the events team as a failing owner: the owner must be a named person inside the function that holds the source system.
Identifies 'TBD, need to sync with sales ops' as meaning the join does not exist, which means the pipeline goal was never actually available.
Identifies 'post-event wrap-up' as a failing read date: the date must be chosen against the funding cycle so the number lands before the decision it feeds.
States that a goal missing any of the four fields is a stated intention, not a goal.
Requires the four fields committed before registration opens, treating Monday as the real deadline for the commitment.
Recommends picking the goal rung the true data-join situation supports instead of keeping the pipeline goal as written.
Asks, or conditions the answer on, whether the developer who attends also signs before any goal ending in a revenue number is stated.
Does not keep both goals as written: a dual goal is only available as the blend, whose three promotion conditions are checked and found unmet here.
States the rejected rungs alongside whatever goal is chosen.
Invents no target pipeline figure and quotes no benchmark number for the exec review.

evals.prompt: Tessro's customer summit is 7 weeks out and registration opens in about 3 weeks. Two things on my plate: first, we're flying in 35 VIP guests - mostly engineering leaders at customer accounts, plus 4 people from federal agencies and 2 from a large bank - covering flights and two hotel nights. Second, RevOps wants the registration feed piped straight into Salesforce so the AEs can work the list during the event. Also legal asked whether we have 'terms' for the event; we've never written any. What do I need signed off, and in what order?
evals.expected_output: The three review items sequenced against the registration and invitation dates, with reversibility stated for each, no jurisdiction or thresholds quoted, and the hosted-guest exposure routed through both companies' rules.
expectations: Names all three review items: legal review of published terms, code of conduct and insurance; privacy review of attendee data moving into sales systems; and anti-bribery/gifting review of hosted guests.
Sequences the privacy review before registration opens, because the notice has to be right at the moment the data is collected - making the 3-week date the binding one.
States that piping the registration feed into the sales systems is a personal-data decision, not a reporting or integration task, owned by whoever holds the company's privacy obligations.
Lists what that privacy review covers: the lawful basis, the notice shown at registration, the retention rule, and the limits on internal reuse.
Names no jurisdiction, statute, or specific retention period, routing the actual rules to the company's own counsel.
States the reversibility asymmetry for the data decision: a list collected under the wrong notice cannot be un-collected, and correction usually means not using what was collected.
Flags the hosted federal-agency and bank guests: the guest's employer's rules are frequently stricter than the host's and are not the host's to waive.
Notes public-sector and regulated-industry guests are the common case where an ordinary hospitality item is not permitted at all.
Quotes no specific gift or hospitality monetary threshold.
Sequences the gifting review before invitations go out, stating that an invitation accepted under a rule it breached cannot be undone by either side.
Notes the goal consequence: a goal that depends on hosting specific accounts depends on those accounts being permitted to accept, so this is asked before the goal is agreed.
States the terms review includes how the code of conduct binds company staff as well as guests, with the enforcement path existing before an incident.
States the terms reversibility: a published term can be revised for the next edition, but an incident at this one cannot be revised at all.

evals.prompt: First-ever HaloForge Summit - we're a platform-engineering startup and the board approved this as a one-time pilot; if it works we might repeat it. My CEO wants us to show BOTH product-adoption movement AND sales pipeline out of it, to get maximum value from the spend. Neither the registration-to-CRM link nor the registration-to-product-analytics link exists yet; we'd have to build both. Our data analyst leaves in October, right after the event. And the CFO keeps saying to pick whatever is cheapest to measure. What goal should we commit to?
evals.expected_output: A single-rung recommendation (adoption-first) that rejects the blend on its three failed conditions, rejects cheapest-to-measure as a criterion, and explains why speed and durability rank the rungs differently.
expectations: Rejects the blended adoption-and-pipeline goal for this edition.

Grounds the blend rejection in its three promotion conditions: a compounding annual program (this is a one-off), both joins existing or buildable, and a named holder of the standing measurement job through the quarter after the event (the analyst is leaving).
States that a blend without a reconciliation owner produces two numbers that disagree and one argument nobody wins.

Names what a cost-first ordering starves: the blend sits top of durability and top of effort, so a cheapest-first reading rejects it every round, and states the condition that would promote it anyway.
States the blend's payoff - a second story to fall back on in a bad quarter - only pays off across editions, never within one, which a one-off cannot collect.

Rejects 'cheapest to measure' as the selection criterion and does not land on goodwill-only for cheapness, noting the cheapest posture is the first to die in a cutback because it has nothing to defend itself with.
States the speed-durability inversion: pipeline is the fastest number to produce and the first to fail, since a quarter with no opportunities leaves nothing to defend the line.
Declines to produce one blended efficiency ranking of the goal rungs, treating the disagreement between the speed and durability orderings as the decision itself.
Recommends adoption-first as the goal for this edition.
States why adoption sits below pipeline on effort despite a slower read: it needs one organisation's data and one approval, where pipeline needs two functions' cooperation.
Requires the four-field commitment before registration opens, with the read date landing before the repeat-or-not decision the pilot feeds.
Flags the departing analyst against the owner field: the metric owner must be a named person still present to report on the read date and through the quarter after the event.
States that a one-off edition tolerates neither the blend's overhead nor a shared funding line's overhead.

evals.prompt: Year 3 of DriftCon - we're Driftline, a CI/CD observability vendor. The whole conference has been funded out of our VP Marketing's budget since year 1. She built it, and she's leaving in January. Product wants in (they demo the roadmap there), DevRel treats it as their flagship, and sales runs an account-dinner track around it. A colleague drafted next year's goals by copying the objectives out of the sponsor prospectus of a conference we exhibit at: 'thought-leadership positioning, brand impressions, qualified lead capture'. How do we set up ownership and goals so DriftCon survives her departure?
evals.expected_output: An ownership redesign that names the sole-owner failure in progress, moves to a multi-function committee with a named executive sponsor, rejects the imported sponsor vocabulary, and demands the handover document now.
expectations: Names the sole-owner failure pattern in progress: the line dies with the person who championed it, and a successor inherits an event they did not choose.
Rejects the sponsor-prospectus goal language, stating the sponsor category set answers what a company buys at somebody else's event and importing it puts a seller's frame on a funder's decision.
Recommends the multi-function committee with a named executive sponsor, given a compounding program and more stakeholding functions (product, DevRel, sales) than one co-fund rung can absorb.
Conditions the committee on confirmed capacity for a standing multi-party report - the political-capital check - not just on stakeholder count.
States the executive sponsor is load-bearing: a committee without one is every veto and none of the protection.
Names the committee failure pattern - assembled for durability, then never convenes, drifting back to sole ownership - and its detection: ask who ran the last review, not who is on the list.
States the committee's real cost: decisions touching audience, date, scope or program become multi-party, and a standing report is owed to each funder in that funder's own terms.
Requires the departing VP's handover document written now: the goal mix with rejected rungs, each funder and what each is buying, the four measurement fields, review status, and re-run triggers.
States the handover is written when the arrangement is made, not on the owner's way out, because the exit version is always the thin one.
Checks the funder-goal coupling per function: sales money tied to a pipeline goal with the join in place, product money tied to an adoption goal.
Brings the same four written lines to every funder - what they get, what it is measured by, what claim they gain, what they do not get - never different lines per funder.
Warns against the no-named-line-owner drift after the departure - funding from whichever discretionary pot has room - deleting it as an option because it fails silently.
Records that a funder joining or leaving, or the goal changing, triggers a re-run of this goal-and-ownership decision, not a growth-planning exercise.
Requires the four-field measurement commitment per chosen goal before registration opens.
